Thermodynamics of the S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet

Taras Hutak Affiliation: Institute for Condensed Matter Physics, National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, Svientsitskii Street 1, 79011 L’viv, Ukraine    Taras Krokhmalskii Affiliation: Institute for Condensed Matter Physics, National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, Svientsitskii Street 1, 79011 L’viv, Ukraine    Jürgen Schnack Affiliation: Fakultät für Physik, Universität Bielefeld, Postfach 100131, 33501 Bielefeld, Germany    Johannes Richter Affiliation: Institut für Physik, Otto-von-Guericke-Universität Magdeburg, P.O. Box 4120, 39016 Magdeburg, Germany Affiliation: Max-Planck-Institut für Physik komplexer Systeme, Nöthnitzer Straße 38, 01187 Dresden, Germany    Oleg Derzhko Affiliation: Institute for Condensed Matter Physics, National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, Svientsitskii Street 1, 79011 L’viv, Ukraine Affiliation: Fakultät für Physik, Universität Bielefeld, Postfach 100131, 33501 Bielefeld, Germany Affiliation: Professor Ivan Vakarchuk Department for Theoretical Physics, Ivan Franko National University of L’viv, Drahomanov Street 12, 79005 L’viv, Ukraine
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet allows to study the interplay of geometrical frustration and quantum as well as thermal fluctuations in three dimensions. We use 16 terms of a high-temperature series expansion complemented by the entropy-method interpolation to examine the specific heat and the uniform susceptibility of this model. We obtain thermodynamic quantities for several possible scenarios determined by the behavior of the specific heat as T→0T\to 0: A power-law decay with the exponent α=1,2\alpha=1,2 and also 33 (gapless energy spectrum) or an exponential decay (gapped energy spectrum). All scenarios give rise to a low-temperature peak in c⁡(T)c(T) (almost a shoulder for α=1\alpha=1) at T<0.05T<0.05, i.e., well below the main high-temperature peak. The functional form of the uniform susceptibility χ⁡(T)\chi(T) below about T=0.5T=0.5 depends strongly not only on the chosen scenario but also on an input parameter χ0≡χ⁡(T=0)\chi_{0}\equiv\chi(T=0). An estimate for the ground-state energy e0e_{0} depends on the adopted specific scenario but is expected to lie between −0.441-0.441 and −0.435-0.435. In addition to the entropy-method interpolation we use the finite-temperature Lanczos method to calculate c⁡(T)c(T) and χ⁡(T)\chi(T) for finite lattices of N=24N=24 and 3636 sites. A combined view on both methods leads us to favor the gapless scenario with α=2\alpha=2 (but α=1\alpha=1 cannot be excluded) and finite χ0\chi_{0} around 0.10.1.

I Introduction

Frustrated quantum spin systems are a subject of intense ongoing research in the field of magnetism [1, 2, 3, 4]. Geometric frustration and quantum fluctuations may prevent any ground-state ordering even in three dimensions. Among several famous examples, the S=1/2S=1/2 pyrochlore-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet has attracted much attention, being for decades a candidate for the realization of a spin-liquid state in three dimensions [5]. After intense numerical studies, a lattice symmetry breaking in the ground state has been revealed [6, 7, 8, 9].

A closely related example is the S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet. Inspired by experiments on the spinel oxide Na4Ir3O8 [10], in which low spin d5d^{5} Ir4+ ions reside on the vertices of a hyperkagome lattice, several theoretical studies for the classical (S→∞S\to\infty) and quantum (S=1/2S=1/2) Heisenberg antiferromagnet on such a lattice have been performed [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. The main focus of these studies is at ground-state properties of the S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet. For the ground state of this model a gapped quantum spin liquid with topological order [12] and a gapless quantum spin liquid with spinon Fermi surfaces [15] were proposed by Lawler et al.. While the former proposal implies a nonzero spin gap, the latter one points to gapless spin excitations. In contrast, Bergholtz et al. [16] proposed a valence bond crystal with a 72 site unit cell as the ground state of this model (thus, breaking translational symmetry but not spin-rotational one). This proposal implies a spin gap with a huge number of singlet excitations below the lowest triplet state and thus a power law for the specific heat and a vanishing susceptibility for vanishing temperature.

The finite-temperature properties of the S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet have also been considered [15, 16, 17, 19]. For the gapless quantum spin liquid of Ref. [15], it was argued that c⁡(T)∝T2c(T)\propto T^{2} at low TT (similar to what is observed for Na4Ir3O8 [10]) and that χ⁡(T)\chi(T) is constant at low TT (again in agreement with experimental data for Na4Ir3O8 [10]). Application of the pseudofermion functional renormalization group [19] also shows that χ⁡(T)\chi(T) exhibits no divergence down to zero temperature, but only a very weak increase. In addition, high-temperature series expansions for cc and χ\chi were developed and compared with the experimental data for Na4Ir3O8 [17].

On the experimental side, apart from the mentioned iridate compound Na4Ir3O8 [10], there are other candidates for a solid-state realization of the hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg anitiferromagnet, see, e.g., Refs. [20, 21, 22]. Note, however, that the 5​d5d-based transition-metal oxides, such as Na4Ir3O8, are known for having a large spin-orbit coupling so that the pure nearest-neighbor Heisenberg Hamiltonian apparently should be augmented by other terms relevant for such materials [23]. Detailed comparisons of c⁡(T)c(T) and χ⁡(T)\chi(T) between theory of Refs. [15, 17, 19] and experimental data for Na4Ir3O8 [10] exhibit noticeable discreapancies roughly below J/2J/2 (JJ is about 300 K for Na4Ir3O8) and even at higher temperatures for the specific heat. The authors attributed this disagreement to an incomplete subtraction of nonmagnetic contribution to the experimentally measured c⁡(T)c(T) [17] and an insufficiency of the spin-isotropic Heisenberg model for description of the S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome antiferromagnet Na4Ir3O8 [16, 23]. Among various spin-anisotropic perturbations one may single out the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya term, Kitaev term, and symmetric exchange anisotropic term [23].

The aim of the present paper is to examine the finite-temperature properties of the S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet – a benchmark model of frustrated quantum magnets. At the moment, we do not intend to compare theoretical findings with experiments since there are no good solid-state examples of such a model yet. There are not so many methods applicable to tackle the thermodynamics of three-dimensional frustrated quantum spin systems. Quantum Monte Carlo suffers from the sign problem [24], exact diagonalization or finite-temperature Lanczos methods are restricted to too small lattices [25, 26, 27], the density-matrix renormalization group technique requires a mapping via a “snake” path to a one-dimensional system [28]. Besides, the pseudofermion functional renormalization group approach focuses on the wave-vector-dependent susceptibility [19], whereas one more universal method, the rotation-invariant Green’s function method [29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35], has not been applied to the S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet so far.

In our study, we utilize the high-temperature series expansions to the order of β16\beta^{16} (β=1/T\beta=1/T) provided by Singh and Oitmaa in Ref. [17]. Singh and Oitmaa used the high-temperature series to compute various thermodynamic properties down to a temperature 11 1 Temperatures are given as multiples of the exchange interaction. T=0.25T=0.25 thus means T/J=0.25T/J=0.25. In our study we set the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg antiferromagnetic interaction J=1J=1. of about T≈0.25T\approx 0.25 [17]. However, this range can be extended down to zero temperature if one combines the series expansion with possible assumptions about the low-energy spectrum of the spin model within the framework of the so-called “entropy method”. The entropy-method interpolation of high-temperature series expansions was suggested by Bernu and Misguish [37] and later used in several studies [38, 39, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, 45]. In the present paper, we unite the series expansion [17] and the entropy method [37, 38, 39, 41, 42, 44] to get the temperature dependence for the specific heat c⁡(T)c(T) and the uniform susceptibility χ⁡(T)\chi(T) of the S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet over the full temperature range. We also obtain a prediction for the ground-state energy of the model e0e_{0}, which provides self-consistency of the entropy-method calculations. Our entropy-method results are accompanied by finite-temperature Lanczos method data for finite lattices up to 36 sites.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II we introduce the model and briefly explain the methods to be used for obtaining the thermodynamic quantities. Then, in Section III, we report our results for the ground-state energy e0e_{0}, the specific heat c⁡(T)c(T), and the uniform susceptibility χ⁡(T)\chi(T). Finally, we summarize our findings in Section IV.

II Model and methods

The hyperkagome lattice has been described in several papers. It can be viewed as a three-dimensional network of corner-sharing triangles with 12 sites in a cubic unit cell. It also can be viewed as a 1/4 depleted pyrochlore lattice, meaning that three out of the four sites in every tetrahedron are occupied by spins. As a result, each spin of the three-dimensional hyperkagome lattice has only four nearest neighbors just as for the two-dimensional kagome lattice. There are several different conventions regarding the coordinates of lattice sites (see, e.g., Refs. [23, 46, 47, 48]). According to Fig. 1, we define the sites on the hyperkagome lattice sites by 𝑹𝒏​α=𝑹𝒏+𝒓α\bm{R}_{\bm{n}\alpha}=\bm{R}_{\bm{n}}+\bm{r}_{\alpha}. Here, 𝑹𝒏=nx​𝒆x+ny​𝒆y+nz​𝒆z\bm{R}_{\bm{n}}=n_{x}\bm{e}_{x}+n_{y}\bm{e}_{y}+n_{z}\bm{e}_{z}, where nx,ny,nzn_{x},n_{y},n_{z} are integers and 𝒆x=(1,0,0)\bm{e}_{x}=(1,0,0), 𝒆y=(0,1,0)\bm{e}_{y}=(0,1,0), 𝒆z=(0,0,1)\bm{e}_{z}=(0,0,1), generates a simple cubic lattice. Moreover, the origins of the 12 equivalent sites in the unit cell may be defined by 𝒓α\bm{r}_{\alpha}, α=1,…,12\alpha=1,\dots,12 with

𝒓1=14​(−2,0,2),𝒓2=14​(−1,3,2),𝒓3=14​(−2,3,1),\displaystyle\bm{r}_{1}{=}\frac{1}{4}\left({-}2,0,2\right),\bm{r}_{2}{=}\frac{1}{4}\left({-}1,3,2\right),\bm{r}_{3}{=}\frac{1}{4}\left({-}2,3,1\right),
𝒓4=14​(−1,1,0),𝒓5=14​(−2,1,3),𝒓6=14​(−1,2,3),\displaystyle\bm{r}_{4}{=}\frac{1}{4}\left({-}1,1,0\right),\bm{r}_{5}{=}\frac{1}{4}\left({-}2,1,3\right),\bm{r}_{6}{=}\frac{1}{4}\left({-}1,2,3\right),
𝒓7=14​(−3,2,1),𝒓8=14​(0,2,2),𝒓9=14​(0,1,1),\displaystyle\bm{r}_{7}{=}\frac{1}{4}\left({-}3,2,1\right),\bm{r}_{8}{=}\frac{1}{4}\left(0,2,2\right),\bm{r}_{9}{=}\frac{1}{4}\left(0,1,1\right),
𝒓10=14​(−3,3,0),𝒓11=(0,0,0),𝒓12=14​(−3,0,3).\displaystyle\bm{r}_{10}{=}\frac{1}{4}\left({-}3,3,0\right),\bm{r}_{11}{=}\left(0,0,0\right),\bm{r}_{12}{=}\frac{1}{4}\left({-}3,0,3\right). (1)

In Fig. 1, we denote 𝒓1,…,𝒓12\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{12} by 1,…,121,\ldots,12. In addition, we display 13 sites of the nearby unit cells by 11−x+y+z11-x+y+z, 11−x+z11-x+z, 8−x8-x and so on, where, e.g., 11−x+y+z11-x+y+z means 𝒓11−𝒆x+𝒆y+𝒆z\bm{r}_{11}-\bm{e}_{x}+\bm{e}_{y}+\bm{e}_{z}, and so on.

In the present paper we consider the isotropic Heisenberg Hamiltonian on the hyperkagome lattice, which is given by

H=∑⟨𝒎​α;𝒏​β⟩𝑺𝒎​α⋅𝑺𝒏​β.H=\sum_{\langle\bm{m}\alpha;\bm{n}\beta\rangle}\bm{S}_{\bm{m}\alpha}\cdot\bm{S}_{\bm{n}\beta}\ . (2)

No extra interactions which may be relevant for solid-state compounds like Na4Ir3O8 are included here, i.e., we treat a kind of idealized minimal model without complicated details but which already provides an interplay between geometrical frustration and quantum and thermal fluctuations. In Eq. (2), the sum runs over the nearest-neighbor bonds of the hyperkagome lattice, and 𝑺𝒎​α\bm{S}_{\bm{m}\alpha} represents the S=1/2S=1/2 spin-vector operator at the lattice site 𝑹𝒎​α\bm{R}_{\bm{m}\alpha}. Expanding the sum in Eq. (2) for fixed 𝒎\bm{m}, one gets 24 bonds, that is, 15 bonds connecting the sites within the unit cell with the same cell index 𝒎\bm{m} and 9 bonds connecting the sites of the unit cell 𝒎\bm{m} with the sites of the neighboring unit cells 𝒎−𝒆x\bm{m}-\bm{e}_{x}, 𝒎−𝒆y\bm{m}-\bm{e}_{y}, 𝒎−𝒆z\bm{m}-\bm{e}_{z}, 𝒎−𝒆x+𝒆y\bm{m}-\bm{e}_{x}+\bm{e}_{y}, 𝒎+𝒆x−𝒆z\bm{m}+\bm{e}_{x}-\bm{e}_{z}, and 𝒎+𝒆y−𝒆z\bm{m}+\bm{e}_{y}-\bm{e}_{z}, see Fig. 1. The remaining 4 bonds in Fig. 1, i.e., the ones which connect the sites 1+y1+y and 12+y12+y, 8−x8-x and 9−x9-x, 9−x9-x and 11−x11-x, 11−x+y+z11-x+y+z and 12+y12+y (cf. the bonds connecting the sites 11 and 1212, 88 and 99, 99 and 1111, 11−x+z11-x+z and 1212), are shown here for the sake of clarity.

It is worth noting that the hyperkagome lattice has similarities with the two-dimensional kagome lattice (corner-sharing triangles in two dimensions), as well as with the three-dimensional pyrochlore lattice (corner-sharing tetrahedrons in three dimensions), which could be considered the “mother” crystal structure, see Fig. 1. An important property is that all three lattices support dispersionless (flat) one-magnon bands. The shortest closed loop on the hyperkagome lattice beyond the triangles is a decagon; it involves ten bonds. The shortest cycle on the kagome and pyrochlore lattices beyond the triangles is a hexagon; it involves six bonds. Since the even regular polygon (decagon or hexagon) is surrounded by equilateral triangles, one expects a localized-magnon state, which lives on a decagon or hexagon, and belongs to a flat band, for more details see Refs. [49, 50].

In the remaining part of this section, we briefly explain the exploited methods: Numerics for finite-size lattices and high-temperature series complemented with the entropy-method interpolation. Here, we only report the key elements necessary to state our results in Sec. III.

First, we determine numerically temperature dependencies for periodic lattices of N=12N=12 sites (exact diagonalization) and N=24, 36N=24,\,36 sites (finite-temperature Lanczos method); for a similar study of the S=1/2S=1/2 pyrochlore-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet see Refs. [51, 42]. Since the unit cell for the hyperkagome lattice contains 12 sites, finite-lattice numerics is restricted to one unit cell [15] and two or three unit cells arranged as a chain. Within the finite-temperature Lanczos method, the sum over an orthonormal basis in the partition function is replaced in a Monte-Carlo fashion by a much smaller sum over RR random vectors where each random vector is employed for a trace estimation [25]. In the present study we take R=200R=200 for N=24N=24 and R=20R=20 for N=36N=36. More details about finite-lattice calculations can be found in Refs. [25, 26, 27, 52, 53]. Our numerical results for finite-size lattices are reported and discussed in Sec. III.

Second, we utilize the high-temperature series expansion up to 16th order, which was reported in Ref. [17] (the Magdeburg HTE code [54, 55] yields the same series of the specific heat and the static uniform susceptibility, however, only up to 13th order), and employ the entropy method [37, 38, 39] to obtain temperature dependencies at all temperatures for infinite lattice.

As is well known, the raw high-temperature series expansion may be improved by simple Padé approximants [u,d]​(T)=Pu​(β)/Qd​(β)[u,d](T)=P_{u}(\beta)/Q_{d}(\beta). Here, Pu​(β)P_{u}(\beta) and Qd​(β)Q_{d}(\beta) are polynomials of order uu and dd, u+d≤16u+d\leq 16, and the series expansion of [u,d]​(T)[u,d](T) coincides with the high-temperature series of cc or χ\chi up to 1616th order with respect to β=1/T\beta=1/T. Comparing close to diagonal Padé approximants in Fig. 2, we conclude that they start to deviate notably one from another below T≈0.5T\approx 0.5 and thus can reproduce the high-temperature peak of c⁡(T)c(T) at T≈0.67T\approx 0.67, but not any of the specific features of χ⁡(T)\chi(T) since χ⁡(T)\chi(T) increases monotonously to temperatures well below T=0.5T=0.5 and also has got its maximum below T=0.5T=0.5.

Within the entropy method [37, 38, 39] one interpolates the entropy (per site) ss as a function of the mean (internal) energy (per site) ee, s⁡(e)s(e). As ee approaches its maximal value e∞=E⁡(T→∞)/N=tr​(H)/N=0e_{\infty}=E(T\rightarrow\infty)/N=\text{tr}(H)/N=0, the entropy is known from high-temperature series expansion, s⁡(e)=ln⁡2+∑i>1ai​eis(e)=\ln 2+\sum_{i>1}a_{i}e^{i} (i.e., the coefficients a2,…,a16a_{2},\ldots,a_{16} are known, see Ref. [37]). As ee approaches its minimal (ground-state) value e0e_{0}, the entropy behaves as s⁡(e)∝(e−e0)α/(1+α)s(e)\propto(e-e_{0})^{\alpha/(1+\alpha)} if c⁡(T)=A​Tαc(T)=AT^{\alpha} for T→0T\to 0 (gapless low-energy excitations) or as s⁡(e)∝−[(e−e0)/Δ]​(ln⁡[Δ⁡(e−e0)]−1)s(e)\propto-[(e-e_{0})/\Delta](\ln[\Delta(e-e_{0})]-1) if c(T)∝e−Δ/T/T2c(T)\propto e^{-\Delta/T}/T^{2} for T→0T\to 0 (gapped low-energy excitations). Next, we interpolate, instead of s⁡(e)s(e), an auxiliary function G⁡(e)G(e), different for the two types of low-energy excitations (the choice of G⁡(e)G(e) was discussed in detail in Refs. [37, 38]), which immediately gives s⁡(e)s(e). Such approximate quantities acquire the subscript “app”. For the gapless case we have

G⁡(e)=[s⁡(e)]1+ααe−e0→Gapp​(e)=(ln⁡2)α1+α−e0​Pu​(e)Qd​(e);\displaystyle G(e){=}\frac{\left[s(e)\right]^{\frac{1+\alpha}{\alpha}}}{e-e_{0}}\to G_{\rm app}(e){=}\frac{\left(\ln 2\right)^{\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}}}{-e_{0}}\frac{P_{u}(e)}{Q_{d}(e)}\ ;
sapp​(e)=[(e−e0)​Gapp​(e)]α1+α.\displaystyle s_{\rm app}(e)=\left[\left(e-e_{0}\right)G_{\rm app}(e)\right]^{\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}}\ . (3)

And for the gapped case we have

G⁡(e)=(e−e0)​[s⁡(e)e−e0]′→Gapp​(e)=ln⁡2e0​Pu​(e)Qd​(e);\displaystyle G(e){=}\left(e-e_{0}\right)\left[\frac{s(e)}{e-e_{0}}\right]^{\prime}\to G_{\rm app}(e){=}\frac{\ln 2}{e_{0}}\frac{P_{u}(e)}{Q_{d}(e)}\ ;
sapp​(e)e−e0=ln⁡2−e0−∫e0d​ξ​Gapp​(ξ)ξ−e0.\displaystyle\frac{s_{\rm app}(e)}{e-e_{0}}=\frac{\ln 2}{-e_{0}}-\int_{e}^{0}{\rm d}\xi\frac{G_{\rm app}(\xi)}{\xi-e_{0}}\ . (4)

Here, Pu​(e)P_{u}(e) and Qd​(e)Q_{d}(e) are the polynomials of order uu and dd, u+d≤16u+d\leq 16, and the series expansion of the quotient [u,d]​(e)=Pu​(e)/Qd​(e)[u,d](e)=P_{u}(e)/Q_{d}(e) coincides with the Maclaurin series of G⁡(e)G(e) known up to 1616th order. Besides, the prime denotes the derivative with respect to ee. Knowing the dependence s⁡(e)s(e), we obtain the desired temperature dependence of the specific heat c⁡(T)c(T) in parametric form: T=1/s′​(e)T=1/s^{\prime}(e) and c=−[s′(e)]2/s′′(e)c=-[s^{\prime}(e)]^{2}/s^{\prime\prime}(e). Finally, we can calculate either the prefactor AA, Aapp=[α1+α/(1+α)α]​[Gapp​(e0)]αA_{\rm app}=[\alpha^{1+\alpha}/(1+\alpha)^{\alpha}][G_{\rm app}(e_{0})]^{\alpha}, for the gapless case or the energy gap Δ\Delta, Δapp=−1/Gapp(e0)\Delta_{\rm app}=-1/G_{\rm app}(e_{0}), for the gapped case. In the presence of a (small) external magnetic field hh one gets the entropy sapp​(e,h)s_{\rm app}(e,h) which yields the uniform susceptibility χ\chi via the relations: m=[1/s′​(e,h)]​∂s⁡(e,h)/∂hm=[1/s^{\prime}(e,h)]\partial s(e,h)/\partial h, χ=m/h\chi=m/h (h→0h\to 0). For further details see Refs. [37, 38, 39, 41, 42, 44].

Thus, to obtain the thermodynamic quantities within the framework of the entropy method one needs, besides the high-temperature series for cc and χ\chi, to know i) the ground-state energy e0e_{0}, ii) how c⁡(T)c(T) vanishes as T→0T\to 0, and iii) the value of χ0≡χ⁡(T=0)\chi_{0}\equiv\chi(T=0) in the case of gapless low-energy excitations. Even if the precise value of e0e_{0} is not available and both gapless and gapped excitations are acceptable, one can proceed as in Ref. [41]. First, one has to assume some reasonable value e0e_{0} in order to explore a certain region of e0e_{0} systematically. Second, one has to assume the exponent α\alpha in the case of a gapless spectrum or one has to assume that the spectrum is gapped. Then, for the assumed e0e_{0} and gapless/gapped energy spectrum one has to calculate within the entropy method the specific heat c⁡(T)c(T) using all nPn_{\rm P} available Padé approximants [u,d]​(e)[u,d](e). There are n+1n+1 Padé approximants based on the series up to nnth order. We discard from the very beginning four Padé approximants [n,0],[n−1,1],[1,n−1],[0,n][n,0],\,[n-1,1],\,[1,n-1],\,[0,n] so that nP=n−3n_{\rm P}=n-3. Next, one has to examine the “closeness” of all nPn_{\rm P} profiles c⁡(T)c(T). To this end, we inspect them thoroughly from some high temperature TiT_{\rm i} down to Tf<TiT_{\rm f}<T_{\rm i} with temperature steps Δ​T\Delta T. If the absolute value of the difference of a certain cc from the arithmetic mean value for this bundle, c¯\overline{c}, at a running temperature TT (Tf≤T≤TiT_{\rm f}\leq T\leq T_{\rm i}) is less than, e.g., 0.001, this cc belongs to the set of “coinciding” Padé approximants. Otherwise, this Padé approximant is discarded and not considered for lower temperatures. According to Refs. [41, 44], a large number of coinciding curves ncPn_{\rm cP}, or more precisely a large value of p=ncP/nPp=n_{\rm cP}/n_{\rm P}, provides evidence that the assumptions made about e0e_{0} and the low-energy excitations are self-consistent.

In Fig. 3 we illustrate such an analysis based on nP=13n_{\rm P}=13 Padé approximants (obtained from the 16th order high-temperature series expansion) in Eqs. (3) or (4) for the specific heat c⁡(T)c(T) under the assumption of a gapless spectrum (blue, red, orange) or a gapped spectrum (green). Here we set Ti=0.5T_{\rm i}=0.5, Δ​T=0.025\Delta T=0.025, Tf=0.1T_{\rm f}=0.1. If e0e_{0} is taken in the range [−0.438 5,−0.435 9][-0.438\,5,-0.435\,9] assuming a gapless spectrum and α=1\alpha=1, i.e., c⁡(T)=A​Tc(T)=AT as T→0T\to 0, we find that ncP=8n_{\text{cP}}=8 and p≈0.62p\approx 0.62. In addition, for the prefactor AA we obtain the interval [5.62,7.74][5.62,7.74]. Similarly, if e0e_{0} is taken in the range [−0.440 2,−0.437 9][-0.440\,2,-0.437\,9] assuming c⁡(T)=A​T2c(T)=AT^{2} as T→0T\to 0, we find that ncP=6n_{\text{cP}}=6, p≈0.46p\approx 0.46, whereas AA belongs to the interval [493,727][493,727]. And for e0e_{0} taken in the range [−0.440 7,−0.438 4][-0.440\,7,-0.438\,4] under the assumption c⁡(T)=A​T3c(T)=AT^{3} as T→0T\to 0, we find ncP=6n_{\text{cP}}=6 and p≈0.46p\approx 0.46. Finally, assuming a gapped spectrum and taking e0e_{0} in the range [−0.438 1,−0.435 3][-0.438\,1,-0.435\,3], we find p=4/13≈0.31p=4/13\approx 0.31. In addition, the energy gap Δ\Delta for the lower e0=−0.438 1e_{0}=-0.438\,1 is 0.0250.025, whereas for the higher e0=−0.435 3e_{0}=-0.435\,3 it is 0.0180.018. All these findings are illustrated in Fig. 3.

Acting in accordance with the strategy of Refs. [41, 44], we may estimate the entropy-method prediction for the ground-state energy e0e_{0} as follows: Under the assumption of gapless excitations, e0e_{0} depends on α\alpha but remains within the range [−0.440 7,−0.435 9][-0.440\,7,-0.435\,9], whereas under the assumption of gapped excitations, e0∈[−0.438 1,−0.435 3]e_{0}\in[-0.438\,1,-0.435\,3]. In what follows, we use this missing input parameter e0e_{0} for the entropy method, considering all assumptions about c⁡(T)c(T) as T→0T\to 0, as well as the minimal and maximal values of e0e_{0} to obtain the shaded areas for c⁡(T)c(T) and χ⁡(T)\chi(T), see Sec. III.2. We note in passing that the uniform susceptibility χ⁡(T)\chi(T) is less convenient for seeking a large value of p=ncP/nPp=n_{\text{cP}}/n_{\rm P}, since it requires the additional parameter χ0\chi_{0} if the spectrum is gapless.

More details about the entropy-method calculations can be found in Refs. [37, 38, 39, 41, 42, 44]. Our entropy-method results are reported and discussed in Sec. III.

III Results

III.1 Ground-state energy e0e_{0}

We begin with the discussion of the ground-state energy of the S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet. Various proposals about the nature of the ground state, i.e., spin liquids or valence-bond crystals, yield e0=−0.424e_{0}=-0.424 [15] or e0=−0.430 115e_{0}=-0.430\,115 [16]. Exact diagonalizations for N=12,24,36N=12,24,36 yield −0.453 74-0.453\,74, −0.446 33-0.446\,33, −0.445 10-0.445\,10, that, apparently, are overestimated values of the thermodynamically large systems. As explained above, to provide consistency of the entropy-method calculations, we have to assume for e0e_{0} the values in the range [−0.441,−0.435][-0.441,-0.435]: This is a combination of several possible scenarios of either a gapless (with α=1,2,3\alpha=1,2,3) or a gapped energy spectrum. Yet another plausible simple approach to determine e0e_{0} from the high-temperature series expansion [6] yields e0e_{0} about −0.448-0.448. The determination of e0e_{0} based on the high-temperature series expansion seems to be rather formal, since it does not use any specific picture for the ground state of the model at hand. However, the experience from other models, including exactly solvable ones and precisely examined numerically ones, gives hints that it may yield quite reasonable predictions [41, 44].

It is worth noting that the ground-state energy for the kagome lattice is quite close: −0.438 6​(5)-0.438\,6(5) [56, 57], −0.438 7-0.438\,7 [58], but for the pyrochlore lattice it is rather different: −0.490​(6)-0.490(6) [6], −0.483 1​(1)-0.483\,1(1) [7], −0.489-0.489 [9].

III.2 Thermodynamic properties

We pass to the finite-temperature properties of the S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet. First, in Fig. 4 we report the temperature dependence of the specific heat c⁡(T)c(T) and the uniform susceptibility χ⁡(T)\chi(T) obtained for finite lattices of N=12, 24, 36N=12,\,24,\,36. Second, in Fig. 5 we report c⁡(T)c(T) and χ⁡(T)\chi(T) obtained by the entropy method. Here, several possibilities, i.e., the gapless spectrum with α=1,2,3\alpha=1,2,3 or the gapped spectrum, were considered, see blue, red, orange, or green curves, respectively. The ground-state energy e0e_{0} was determined from the analysis of c⁡(T)c(T) as was explained in Sec. II. We used [8,8]​(e)[8,8](e) in Eqs. (3) or (4) as well as the region of e0e_{0} where pp has a maximum, see Fig. 3, in order to estimate the spread of the derived functions. For the gapless excitations we set χ0=0, 0.08, 0.12, 0.16\chi_{0}=0,\,0.08,\,0.12,\,0.16.

Let us now discuss the thermodynamic quantities of the S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet in some detail. As it follows from the upper panel of Fig. 4, the high-temperature peak of the specific heat does not show any finite-size scaling; it is already provided by the calculations for one unit cell (N=12N=12). On these grounds, we thus speculate that the curve of the specific heat at temperatures of the high-temperature peak and above represents the thermodynamic limit 22 2 In contrast, the results for the S=1/2S=1/2 pyrochlore-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet of N=32N=32 sites [42] reflect the thermodynamic limit only for T>0.7T>0.7, well above the temperature of the high-temperature peak of c⁡(T)c(T). Therefore, the finite-lattice results for the hyperkagome case allow a reliable discussion of thermodynamic properties for much lower temperatures down to T≈0.2T\approx 0.2., see also N=36N=36 data in Fig. 5. The position of the low-temperature peak, on the other hand, does depend on the size. Moreover, the height decreases notably with growing NN. The results of the entropy method in Fig. 5 refer to the infinite lattice. As it follows from the upper panel of Fig. 5, the specific heat c⁡(T)c(T) besides the high-temperature peak at T≈0.67T\approx 0.67 has an additional low-temperature maximum, which is about two times smaller and occurs below T=0.05T=0.05 under both assumptions of gapless and gapped excitations. For the case of the gapless excitations with α=1\alpha=1, the low-temperature peak is so small that it is perceived as a shoulder, see the blue curve in the upper panel of Fig. 5.

As can be seen in the lower panel of Fig. 4, the maximum of χ⁡(T)\chi(T) has a mild dependence on system size. Moreover, the height remains practically unchanged. This behavior can be traced back to the size of the singlet-triplet gap for these systems. Its value is Δs−t≈0.383,0.216,0.136\Delta_{\rm s{-}t}\approx 0.383,0.216,0.136 for N=12,24,36N=12,24,36, respectively. According to the entropy-method analysis reported in the lower panel of Fig. 5, the uniform susceptibility χ⁡(T)\chi(T) behaves identically at TT above about 0.50.5 for gapless and gapped excitations. For lower temperatures, the behavior of χ⁡(T)\chi(T) depends on the adopted scenario and the χ0\chi_{0} value for gapless excitations. In the case of gapless spin excitations, the uniform susceptibility approaches χ0>0\chi_{0}>0 as T→0T\to 0 and displays or does not display a maximum roughly below T=0.3T=0.3 depending on the specific value χ0\chi_{0}, cf. blue, red, orange curves in the lower panel of Fig. 5.

An important general message that can be taken from Fig. 5 is that the entropy-method and finite-system numerical data (and even simple Padé approximants for χ\chi) favor the assumption of a gapless spectrum and a quadratically vanishing specific heat at low temperature with finite χ0\chi_{0} around 0.10.1. However, a linear decay of the specific heat cannot be excluded.

It is worthy to put our results for the hyperkagome lattice in the context of prior work for the kagome and pyrochlore lattices. Concerning c⁡(T)c(T) (the upper panels of Figs. 4 and 5), its features at least at intermediate temperatures and above, are quite similar to what is known for the kagome-lattice and also the square-kagome-lattice case (a peak at T=0.67T=0.67, a shoulder of two times smaller height for 0.1<T<0.250.1<T<0.25 [60, 61]), but differ from those for the pyrochlore-lattice case, where only one peak in c⁡(T)c(T), but no additional low-temperature feature such as peak or shoulder was found [42, 62]. Concerning χ⁡(T)\chi(T) (the lower panels of Figs. 4 and 5), it resembles the maximum of χ⁡(T)\chi(T) for the finite-size kagome lattices [60] and for the infinite kagome lattice analyzed by the entropy method [39]. In contrast, for the pyrochlore lattice we have several scenarios, none of which can be excluded to date [63, 42, 62]. Thus, we may conclude that the three-dimensional hyperkagome lattice is closer to highly frustrated two-dimensional lattices (kagome, square-kagome) than to the three-dimensional pyrochlore lattice. However, it is worth noting the difference: For the kagome lattice the low-temperature peak of c⁡(T)c(T) moves to higher temperatures with increasing NN [60], opposite to what is observed for the hyperkagome lattice (recall the top panel of Fig. 4). Thus, for the kagome lattice one yields a low-temperature shoulder of the main peak in the thermodynamic limit [64].

IV Summary and outlook

In the present paper, we used finite-lattice calculations and high-temperature series expansions up to 16th order [17] complemented by plausible assumptions about low-temperature properties according to the entropy method to obtain the specific heat c⁡(T)c(T) and the uniform susceptibility χ⁡(T)\chi(T) of the S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet at all temperatures. Finite-lattice calculations are suitable to discuss the thermodynamics above T=0.2T=0.2, cf. N=24N=24 and N=36N=36 data in Fig. 4. The entropy method requires the knowledge of ground state and low-energy excitations which is currently not available. Therefore, we tested several scenarios (gapless excitations with various exponents for a power-law decay of c⁡(T→0)c(T\to 0) and values of χ0\chi_{0} or gapped excitations) and examined the coherence of the obtained results. Our main findings are as follows. We observe a low-temperature peak in c⁡(T)c(T) (almost a shoulder for α=1\alpha=1) at T<0.05T<0.05, i.e., well below the main high-temperature peak. χ⁡(T)\chi(T) below T=0.5T=0.5 relies heavily on the adopted scenario. Combining finite-lattice and entropy-method results gives evidence in favor of gapless spin excitations with a quadratic low-temperature specific heat decay (although a linear one cannot be ruled out) and finite χ\chi at T=0T=0 around 0.10.1. Such results agree with the proposal of a gapless quantum spin liquid in Ref. [15] and the pseudofermion functional renormalization group study of Ref. [19]. As a byproduct, we have extracted the ground-state energy e0e_{0} with a procedure explained in Sec. II. Although the value of e0e_{0} depends on the adopted scenario, it was always restricted to [−0.441,−0.435][-0.441,-0.435]. We have found that the thermodynamics of the three-dimensional hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet is quite similar to the two-dimensional kagome-lattice one, but differs from that on the pyrochlore lattice.

Future work on the thermodynamics of the S=1/2S=1/2 hyperkagome-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet may be related to application of specific tools to tackle the problem. For instance, this model represents a so-called flat-band system: The one-magnon energy spectrum has a fourfold degenerate dispersionless band, which is the lowest-energy band. The flat-band states will be relevant at high fields and low temperatures and their dominant contribution to thermodynamics can be elaborated by special methods of flat-band systems, see Refs. [49, 50]. Such a program has been realized for the S=1/2S=1/2 kagome-lattice and pyrochlore-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnets in Refs. [65, 66], and it might be applicable here, too.
